newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn minister says mark correction overdone.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn minister says mark correction overdone.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt on Wednesday said he thought the recent weakness of the mark was a normal market correction but that this was now overdone.
"What is happening now is partly a normalisation. The swings are exaggerated," Rexrodt told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet discussed the mark's recent slide against the dollar and sterling in the run-up to Europe's planned single currency during its meeting on Wednesday, he said.

When asked whether the cabinet would issue a statement on currency developments, he said: "Perhaps the economic fundamentals in the Anglo-Saxon countries are better ...," but then stopped short and added: "Cabinet discussed this."

The government is widely expected to comment on recent foreign exchange developments at its regular news conference in the afternoon and state its commitment to a strong mark ahead of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Germany is growing increasingly concerned that the debate about EMU is shaking the confidence of financial markets in the strong mark, threatening to tarnish the symbol of the country's postwar prosperity.

Any statement by the government would mark the next phase in Germany's battle to assure financial markets that it wants the mark to reach EMU as a strong currency and the euro single currency to be as strong.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday said the recent weakening of what has been a rock solid currency for nearly half a century was an overreaction of financial markets concerned about European monetary union.

Waigel's rare foray on to the foreign exchange battlefield caused the dollar to stumble temporarily but the U.S. currency quickly regained its footing and in the evening Waigel renewed his warnings and set the stage for the next attack.
He said markets had overreacted in pushing the dollar and sterling to multi-year highs and hinted that the Group of Seven rich industrialised nations could be prepared to take corrective action.

Waigel's support for the mark came hot on the heels of similar statements from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer last week but failed to hold the dollar back as it soared to 71-month highs above 1.80 marks.

The G7 industrialised nations, which in 1995 called for an "orderly reversal" of the dollar from record lows near 1.3450 marks, signalled in February -- when the dollar rate was about 1.65 marks -- that the recovery had gone about far enough.
Analysts have blamed the mark's weakness on a row in Germany over how strictly entry criteria for EMU should be interpreted. They said this has discredited both the planned euro and the mark itself.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler, also speaking late on Tuesday, said the mark's appreciation against other currencies might have become somewhat excessive.

"The appreciation of the deutschemark has been corrected in the meantime and that may even go somewhat beyond a correction," Zeitler told a regional business seminar in Bavaria. He did not specify what exchange rates he was referring to in regard to the mark's movements.
The mark's weakness comes at a critical point for Germany, with the planned launch of the European single currency now less than 18 months away.
Tietmeyer said it was essential that the mark go into the joint currency from a position of strength. Strategic use of a weak currency to promote trade is anathema to inflation-conscious Germans.
But wrangling over the precise fiscal criteria for monetary union -- and the various accounting methods to reach them -- has damaged the credibility of the euro and of the mark.
Economists said the current currency situation no longer reflected the strength of the dollar or of sterling, but the weakness of the mark.
-- william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150)
